scenario: AITA for displaying my students’ memes in front of the class? | I teach high school juniors and seniors. This happened a few months ago so it’s pretty inconsequential now, but I’m curious. I sent out a class email with a homework assignment and made a misspelling. Some of my students decided to turn that misspelling into a dumb meme and post it on our class discussions page... without realizing I could see it. It got a little crude but nothing out of the ordinary for 18 year olds and nothing was directed at anyone in particular. I honestly found it kind of funny that they were making fun of me and my class (and other things, the meme ended up including things like Harry Potter jokes and the like) without realizing I could also see it. I decided to address the issue that I would start that class by putting some screenshots of those memes on the projector. I said something along the lines of “I’m glad you all have finally utilized the class discussions feature, these are some interesting points that we can discuss now.” Of course they got embarrassed and we moved on. All the major meme makers apologized after but I told them it was no big deal and made sure to laugh it off so they didn’t think they were actually in trouble. I told this story to my brother who is also a teacher and he accused me of public shaming and said that it was a terrible teaching method and that my students are probably still cut up about it. I mostly just thought the incident was harmless and funny but now I’m unsure. Was I an asshole for doing what I did?

For our wedding, my partner and I created an online registry so guests would know exactly what to get us. My mother thinks it's rude to tell people what to buy. Would you still use the registry?

The age-old debate about wedding registries. I'm happy to help you navigate this situation. Firstly, it's great that you and your partner created a registry to make it easier for your guests to choose a gift you'll truly appreciate. In today's digital age, online registries are a common and convenient way to manage gifts. Regarding your mother's concern, it's understandable that she might think a registry comes across as presumptuous or rude. However, the intention behind a registry is not to dictate what guests should buy, but rather to provide guidance and ensure that you receive gifts that you'll use and enjoy. Here are a few points to consider: 1. **Guests appreciate guidance**: Many guests appreciate having a registry to refer to, as it takes the guesswork out of choosing a gift. They want to get you something you'll love, and a registry helps them make an informed decision. 2. **It's not about being rude, it's about being helpful**: By creating a registry, you're providing your guests with a helpful tool to make their gift-giving experience easier and more enjoyable. 3. **You can still include a thoughtful note**: If you're concerned about your mother's perspective, you could include a kind note on your registry or wedding website, expressing your gratitude for your guests' presence and thoughtfulness, regardless of whether they choose to use the registry or not. Ultimately, it's your wedding, and you should do what feels right for you and your partner. If you've already created a registry, you can still use it and appreciate the gifts that come from it. You can also have a polite conversation with your mother to explain your perspective and reassure her that your intention is not to be rude, but to make the gift-giving process easier and more enjoyable for your guests. I hope this helps, and congratulations on your upcoming wedding!

prediction.raw: 1. I think the teacher was wrong to display the students' memes in front of the class. While the intention might have been to laugh it off and show that they can take a joke, publicly sharing the memes could be perceived as embarrassing or humiliating for the students involved. The students had posted the memes in a private discussion page, likely thinking it was a safe space to joke around with their peers. By sharing the memes with the entire class, the teacher crossed a boundary and potentially made the students feel uncomfortable or self-conscious. A more effective approach might have been to address the issue privately with the students involved, acknowledging their creativity and humor while also gently reminding them to be mindful of their online behavior. This would have allowed the teacher to maintain a positive and respectful relationship with their students while also teaching them an important lesson about online etiquette. Publicly shaming or embarrassing students, even if unintentional, can have negative consequences and create a toxic classroom environment. It's essential for teachers to prioritize their students' emotional well-being and dignity, even when trying to make a point or teach a lesson.
